lessons.title: Interchange a nonnegative series and expectation
lessons.reviewNote: MCT applies to the increasing partial sums and permits an infinite value. For signed terms, finite sum of absolute expectations is sufficient, via Tonelli then Fubini.

lessons.title: Transfer: a parameterized integral limit
lessons.reviewNote: Pointwise convergence plus the single integrable envelope e^(−x) verifies every DCT hypothesis. The integral of the limit is one.

lessons.title: Verify Cauchy–Schwarz on atoms
lessons.reviewNote: Both variables are in L2 on the finite space. Equality for nonzero norms requires proportional absolute values; the primary vectors are not proportional. If either norm is zero, both sides are zero.

lessons.title: Prove Hölder by Young
lessons.reviewNote: Conjugate exponents are exactly 3 and 3/2. The finite moment assumptions ensure the norms exist; zero-norm and equality cases are stated separately.

lessons.title: Jensen from a supporting line
lessons.reviewNote: For a finite convex function, a subgradient exists at an interior mean; the supporting-line proof requires E[X] and E[φ(X)] to be defined. Strictness follows when the support line inequality is strict on a positive-probability set.

lessons.title: Counterexample: L1 does not imply L2
lessons.reviewNote: The normalizer is c=1/ζ(3). The first-moment series is ζ(2), while the second-moment series is harmonic and divergent; X is nonnegative so its expectation is unambiguous.

lessons.title: Transfer: interpolate moments
lessons.reviewNote: Hölder uses q=p/r and q′=p/(p−r); both exceed one and are conjugate. The probability assumption supplies E[1]=1; the counting-measure companion exhibits the missing finite-mass factor.

lessons.title: Factor a product law
lessons.reviewNote: The four-point Bernoulli law factors only because independence is given. All primary payoffs are bounded, so the expectation identity is finite.

lessons.title: Prove Borel–Cantelli I
lessons.reviewNote: Tail unions decrease to the i.o. event; finite probability measure gives continuity from above. The first Borel–Cantelli conclusion needs no independence.

lessons.title: Prove Borel–Cantelli II
lessons.reviewNote: For each tail, independence is used to factor the finite no-event probability; 1−p≤e^(−p) and divergence force the limit to zero. Continuity from above then applies.

lessons.title: Counterexample without independence
lessons.reviewNote: This repeated-event example has divergent sum but only half probability of infinitely many occurrences. The nested-uniform companion has i.o. probability zero; both show why independence matters for the second lemma.

lessons.title: Transfer: summable errors imply almost-sure convergence
lessons.reviewNote: Countability of positive rational thresholds is what preserves a probability-one intersection. The third example checks a.s. convergence while its expectations stay one, exposing the need for additional integrability to pass limits through expectations.

lessons.title: Compute on a finite partition
lessons.reviewNote: Each block in the primary partition has positive probability 1/2, so its conditional mean is uniquely determined by the block integral. Additivity extends the check from generating blocks to every G-event.

lessons.title: Prove uniqueness a.s.
lessons.reviewNote: The proof uses integrability to define each difference integral and G-measurability of level sets. Testing both signs makes the exceptional set {Z≠W} a countable union of null sets.

lessons.title: Derive the two-block RN density
lessons.reviewNote: Both blocks have positive probability by hypothesis, so division is legal. The constructed block-constant variable is integrable because its block integrals are finite for X in L1.

lessons.title: Counterexample: versions differ at a null point
lessons.reviewNote: The null modification preserves every event integral because the changed point has probability zero. Measurability remains a separate requirement; the trivial-sigma-field check shows that integral agreement alone is insufficient.
lessons.priorCorrection: Ambient measurability does not imply G-measurability.

lessons.title: Transfer: extend identities to bounded test functions
lessons.reviewNote: Uniform simple approximation is valid for bounded measurable H. Integrability of X and its conditional expectation controls the approximation error; for unbounded H, the product expectations may not exist.

lessons.title: Tower on nested finite partitions
lessons.reviewNote: The primary partitions are nested, and each block has positive probability. The tower property is asserted up to a.s. equality, as conditional expectations are versions.

lessons.title: Prove tower property
lessons.reviewNote: The proof tests each H-event and then invokes uniqueness; integrability follows from X in L1 and the conditional-expectation construction.

lessons.title: Prove the L² orthogonality identity
lessons.reviewNote: To extend beyond simple H, first use conditional Jensen to place Z in L2, then Cauchy–Schwarz passes the inner product through L2 approximation.

lessons.title: Calculate the projection risk decomposition
lessons.reviewNote: The risk expansion uses equal atom masses and completes squares around each block mean. The minimum risk is the within-block residual variance; fitted block means are unique.

lessons.title: Transfer: pull out a measurable multiplier
lessons.reviewNote: Bounded G-measurability makes H times X integrable; conditional Jensen gives integrability of H E[X|G]. The proof verifies candidate integrals before invoking uniqueness.

lessons.title: Classify four convergence claims
lessons.reviewNote: For the independent rare-event case, the L1 norm tends to zero while almost-sure convergence fails; these modes are compatible. At U=0 the first sequence stays one, but this is a null singleton.

lessons.title: Prove a.s. implies probability convergence
lessons.reviewNote: Continuity from above needs decreasing events and a finite first measure; probability measures satisfy this. The current-error-to-tail-union inclusion is what returns the tail limit to each original probability.

lessons.title: Probability convergence without a.s. convergence
lessons.reviewNote: Borel–Cantelli II needs independence and a divergent sum; both are stated in the primary. The square-summable companion correctly uses lemma I without independence.

lessons.title: Lᵖ convergence implies probability convergence
lessons.reviewNote: Markov requires a nonnegative integrable variable and a strictly positive threshold. The implication works for every p>0; in the usual Lp space notation one often assumes p≥1.

lessons.title: Transfer: uniqueness of probability limits
lessons.reviewNote: The event inclusion and union bound apply for each fixed epsilon; the a.s. conclusion uses countably many thresholds 1/k. The companions check both equal and unequal limit candidates directly.

lessons.title: Test UI for bounded and spiky families
lessons.reviewNote: For the spike, the supremum is exactly one: a chosen n>K attains one and no tail expectation can exceed the full mean one. Bounded families have identically zero tails beyond their common bound.

lessons.title: Prove the bounded-probability-to-L¹ lemma
lessons.reviewNote: The split yields a limsup bound by each fixed epsilon; the correct order is n→∞ first and epsilon↓0 second. Boundedness of both variables is needed for the $2K$ bound.

lessons.title: Show the spike violates Vitali conclusion
lessons.reviewNote: The moving-spike computations distinguish bounded first moments from UI: each expectation is one, yet tail mass stays one at an index chosen beyond any threshold. Endpoints do not affect Lebesgue probabilities.

lessons.title: Derive L¹ convergence from UI by truncation
lessons.reviewNote: The proof sketch needs the standard subsequence principle (probability convergence yields an a.s.-convergent subsequence) and Fatou for the lower-semicontinuous function $xmapsto|x|1_{{|x|>K}}$. UI also bounds first moments, so Fatou first establishes X integrable. Source theorem is presented as a sourced proof sketch, not reproved from the beginning.

lessons.title: Transfer: bounded moments imply UI
lessons.reviewNote: The pointwise inequality is valid for K>0 and p>1. A uniform pth-moment bound gives an explicit tail rate $C K^{-(p-1)}$, which tends to zero uniformly over the family.

lessons.title: Prove the finite-variance WLLN
lessons.reviewNote: The variance calculation needs independence (uncorrelatedness would suffice for this step) and a finite common variance; Chebyshev then proves convergence in probability only.

lessons.title: Compare modes on Bernoulli sample means
lessons.reviewNote: The Chebyshev result uses finite variance and independence. Almost-sure convergence is a separate SLLN application, valid because Bernoulli variables have finite first moment.

lessons.title: Use Borel–Cantelli to upgrade a tail bound
lessons.reviewNote: Borel–Cantelli I needs no independence. Countability lets all rational-threshold conclusions hold on one common probability-one set; a single threshold cannot establish arbitrary closeness.

lessons.title: Diagnose dependence in a sample mean
lessons.reviewNote: Positive variance ensures at least one positive deviation threshold has nonzero probability. Covariance terms remain nonzero under perfect dependence, so the iid variance formula cannot be used.

lessons.title: Transfer: bounded iid variables and SLLN scope
lessons.reviewNote: The boundedness assumption supplies both finite variance for the Chebyshev WLLN and finite first absolute moment for the cited Kolmogorov SLLN. The SLLN implication is explicitly sourced rather than attributed to the WLLN proof.

lessons.title: Check characteristic functions
lessons.reviewNote: The characteristic function is an expectation of a bounded complex variable; the finite-support computations require no moment assumptions. Continuity at zero is checked directly.

lessons.title: Apply Slutsky without independence
lessons.reviewNote: I repaired the primary prompt by requiring the ratio to be defined almost surely at each n; convergence to −1 alone only makes zero denominators negligible asymptotically, not automatically legal in a finite-n quotient. Slutsky needs no independence.

lessons.title: Counterexample: weak convergence does not imply mean convergence
lessons.reviewNote: The weak-convergence check uses bounded continuous test functions; the identity x is unbounded and therefore is not controlled. The explicit tail supremum demonstrates failure of UI.

lessons.title: Prove a continuous mapping for a monotone transform
lessons.reviewNote: The inverse-CDF identity is restricted to y in the range; continuity points of the transformed CDF correspond to acceptable inverse thresholds. The discontinuous indicator companion fails exactly at the limit point zero.

lessons.title: Transfer: identify a missing moment condition
lessons.reviewNote: The standard weak-convergence-plus-UI result is the stated sufficient condition; the rare-spike counterexample has weak limit zero but expectation one. Uniform boundedness makes the sequence UI, and weak limits remain supported on the same closed bounded interval.

lessons.title: Standardize a Bernoulli sum
lessons.reviewNote: The standardization uses variance p(1−p)/n; for count thresholds the continuity correction shifts by half a count. Numerical normal tails are approximations, not exact binomial probabilities.

lessons.title: Derive the characteristic-function expansion
lessons.reviewNote: The finite second moment is sufficient; no third absolute moment is used. The global second-order remainder bound and truncation justify the little-o expansion under exactly the stated mean and variance assumptions.

lessons.title: Check the normalized-sum characteristic function
lessons.reviewNote: The expansion is applied at fixed t, with iid centered variance-one summands. The limit characteristic function is continuous at zero, the needed Lévy condition.

lessons.title: Counterexample: the variance hypothesis fails
lessons.reviewNote: For a tail exponent α, the rth absolute moment is finite exactly when r<α in this Pareto-tail range. Here α=3/2 gives finite first moment but infinite second moment; no stable-law conclusion is asserted.

lessons.title: Transfer: asymptotic interval and its limits
lessons.reviewNote: The Wald interval is a pointwise asymptotic approximation for fixed interior p, not a uniform finite-sample guarantee. Near the boundary its plug-in standard error can degenerate and the interval may leave [0,1].

lessons.title: Solve a stationary distribution
lessons.reviewNote: Stationarity is a row-vector equation and differs from updating a nonstationary initial law. Each example solves one coordinate plus normalization and checks invariance.

lessons.title: Prove total-variation contraction
lessons.reviewNote: The convention here is $|mu-eta|_{TV}=sup_A|mu(A)-eta(A)|= rac12sum_i|mu_i-eta_i|$ on finite states. With this convention a Markov kernel contracts by factor at most one.

lessons.title: Verify the common minorization
lessons.reviewNote: Minorization means coordinatewise domination of the same probability measure by every row. Subtraction must leave nonnegative entries, and division by 1−ε must restore row sum one.

lessons.title: Counterexample: periodic alternation
lessons.reviewNote: Invariance alone does not imply convergence from every initial law. Disjoint row supports prevent any shared positive probability component, so the Doeblin contraction hypothesis fails.

lessons.title: Transfer: geometric mixing bound
lessons.reviewNote: The estimate iterates the one-step contraction and assumes π is invariant. Since the contraction factor is below one for ε>0, the bound tends geometrically to zero.

lessons.title: Verify a martingale in a two-step tree
lessons.reviewNote: The martingale condition concerns conditional means given the past, not merely the unconditional mean of the whole process. Finite trees guarantee integrability in these examples.

lessons.title: Prove bounded optional stopping
lessons.reviewNote: Bounded stopping means a deterministic horizon N, not merely almost-sure finiteness. Predictability of each activation indicator is the key conditional-expectation step.

lessons.title: Use conditional orthogonality of increments
lessons.reviewNote: The later increment has conditional mean zero and the earlier increment is measurable at that conditioning time. Square integrability supplies product integrability for the conditional-expectation calculation.

lessons.title: Counterexample: unbounded stopping breaks expectation preservation
lessons.reviewNote: I preserved the gambler’s-ruin proof rather than asserting recurrence: finite-interval exits are bounded stops, and their exact upper-exit probabilities approach one. The one-sided stopped family is not UI, as shown by its a.s. limit 1 versus expectation 0 at every truncation.

lessons.title: Transfer: finite-horizon stopping decomposition
lessons.reviewNote: The pathwise stopped-sum identity includes increment k exactly on ${	auge k}$, which is measurable at time k−1 for a stopping time. A rule based on the sign of the increment itself is not predictable.

lessons.title: Dominated limit and escaping mass
lessons.reviewNote: DCT requires a.e. convergence and one integrable dominator. The primary spike has integral one and no such dominator; companions check both dominated convergence and escaping mass.

lessons.title: Tower and uniqueness of conditional expectation
lessons.reviewNote: Nesting lets both defining integral identities apply to the same H-events. Uniqueness is almost sure; changing a version on a null set preserves validity.

lessons.title: Distinguish WLLN from SLLN
lessons.reviewNote: Chebyshev proves convergence in probability under iid finite variance; the iid SLLN needs only finite first absolute moment. The dependent Rademacher sequence shows why independence cannot be dropped.

lessons.title: Finite-chain invariant law and mixing
lessons.reviewNote: The invariant distributions were checked by multiplication. Each stated rowwise lower bound leaves nonnegative residual rows of total mass one after division by epsilon, so the TV contraction hypotheses hold.

lessons.title: Bounded versus unbounded stopping
lessons.reviewNote: The bounded proof relies on predictable inclusion events and a finite sum. The primary first-hit time is a.s. finite but unbounded; the companions distinguish this from cases where bounded stopped values justify a limit by dominated convergence.

lessons.title: Check identifiability in a Bernoulli model
lessons.reviewNote: Identifiability is injectivity of the map from parameter to probability law. The Bernoulli endpoints are identifiable; the signed-square map fails for every nonzero sign pair.

lessons.title: Prove sufficiency factorization on finite support
lessons.reviewNote: The finite-support factorization is equivalent to parameter-free conditional laws on positive-probability T-fibers. The common-support assumption permits a shared sample-space comparison; zero-probability fibers are excluded from conditioning.

lessons.title: Factor a binomial likelihood
lessons.reviewNote: The Bernoulli likelihood factorization is valid on the common binary sample space, including boundary parameters by the usual pmf convention. Conditional on the count, all strings have equal probability.

lessons.title: Counterexample: a statistic can discard identifiable information
lessons.reviewNote: The conditional-law criterion directly detects lost information in each example; the primary uses an interior Bernoulli parameter so the conditioning event always has positive probability. Identifiability concerns the whole law and is a different property.

lessons.title: Transfer: exponential-family sufficient statistic
lessons.reviewNote: The Poisson sum is sufficient by factorization on the common countable support, and its mean identifies the parameter. The companions separately verify continuous and discrete exponential-family factorizations.

lessons.title: Rao–Blackwellize a Bernoulli observation
lessons.reviewNote: For Bernoulli data the conditional success chance is t/n on every fiber, including the two endpoints. Variance comparisons use the exact binomial variance; companion conditional means follow exchangeability.

lessons.title: Prove the conditional-variance improvement
lessons.reviewNote: The cross term vanishes by conditioning on T, requiring square integrability for the variance quantities. Equality in the reduction occurs precisely when U is already T-measurable a.s.

lessons.title: Use completeness to prove uniqueness
lessons.reviewNote: The uniqueness argument requires zero expectation for every parameter and integrability of the difference. Binomial and Poisson companions show coefficient arguments underlying completeness; the normal completeness premise is explicitly assumed.

lessons.title: Counterexample: sufficiency without completeness
lessons.reviewNote: Each noncompleteness witness is nonzero on a value with positive probability and has expectation zero at every allowed parameter. Sufficiency follows separately from the likelihood factorization.

lessons.title: Transfer: verify a UMVU claim
lessons.reviewNote: The UMVU proof compares against every unbiased finite-variance estimator, using sufficiency for Rao–Blackwell and completeness for uniqueness. The binomial-completeness theorem is expressly named as assumed, not proved.

lessons.title: Build a randomized most-powerful test
lessons.reviewNote: For the primary pair the high-ratio outcome exactly uses the level, so no randomization is needed. Companion randomization probabilities are computed from the remaining null mass, then power is evaluated under the alternative.

lessons.title: Prove the Neyman–Pearson inequality
lessons.reviewNote: The proof needs a common dominating measure, randomized tests in [0,1], an exact-size LR rule, and nonnegative k. Integrating the pointwise inequality gives the claimed power ordering for simple-versus-simple hypotheses.

lessons.title: Derive a likelihood-ratio ordering
lessons.reviewNote: The monotonicity conclusion assumes interior probabilities so the binomial likelihood ratio is finite. If the alternative probability is smaller, the LR decreases and the NP region is a lower tail; discrete levels may require boundary randomization.

lessons.title: Counterexample: composite alternatives
lessons.reviewNote: The primary is an explicit normal counterexample: for alpha=.05, the two simple alternatives +1 and -1 have different unique NP tails. This refutes a general UMP claim while leaving open one-sided UMP and restricted unbiased/invariant optimality results.
lessons.priorCorrection: Symmetry does not generally provide a two-sided UMP test.

lessons.title: Transfer: compare tests by size and power
lessons.reviewNote: The primary optimization is over randomized tests with both rejection probabilities between zero and one. Likelihood-ratio ordering shows X=1 gets the size budget first; the stated linear bound verifies no feasible pair exceeds power .6.

lessons.title: Compute score and information for Bernoulli
lessons.reviewNote: The score and information formulas assume an interior parameter and the usual fixed support of the Bernoulli model. The score is centered, so its variance and second moment agree.

lessons.title: Prove the Cramér–Rao inequality
lessons.reviewNote: The normalization derivative and estimator-mean derivative require separate domination arguments; common support alone is not enough, especially for unbounded T. Cauchy–Schwarz additionally needs finite estimator variance and positive finite score information.

lessons.title: Check equality for the sample proportion
lessons.reviewNote: The CR comparisons use unbiased estimators and regular fixed-support models. Equality holds because each centered estimator is a constant multiple of its score, not merely because the numeric variances happen to match.

lessons.title: Counterexample: parameter-dependent support
lessons.reviewNote: The specified endpoint-inclusive density makes the Uniform(0,theta) likelihood attain its maximum at the sample maximum. The moving support breaks the zero-mean score identity; the unbiased rescaling $(n+1)M/n$ has variance $	heta^2/[n(n+2)]<	heta^2/n^2$, exposing why the formal regular CR bound cannot be used.
lessons.priorCorrection: Derive maximum-order-statistic moments and specify the likelihood endpoint convention.

lessons.title: Transfer: score identities under reparameterization
lessons.reviewNote: The information transformation squares the inverse-map derivative. The CR bound is for an unbiased estimator of eta and presumes the reparameterized family retains the regularity hypotheses.

lessons.title: Prove epsilon separation for an approximate maximizer
lessons.reviewNote: The contradiction compares the empirical score outside the epsilon set with the score at the feasible target and then subtracts the optimization tolerance. Positivity of the population separation gap is essential; pointwise uniqueness alone does not supply this numerical bound.

lessons.title: Constrained Bernoulli likelihood consistency
lessons.reviewNote: The finite-sample constrained maximizer is the clipped sample proportion, including all-success and all-failure data; consistency uses IID sampling and an interior true probability. The restriction 0<a<1/2 keeps the likelihood finite on the whole parameter interval.
lessons.priorCorrection: Boundary samples still give a strictly concave Bernoulli log likelihood on the interior.

lessons.title: Pointwise convergence can miss a moving spike
lessons.reviewNote: Pointwise convergence is verified by eventual exclusion of each fixed parameter from the moving intervals; inconsistent argmax requires the spike height to beat every off-spike value. The shrinking locations and positive score margins make that comparison explicit.

lessons.title: Prove a uniform law using finite nets
lessons.reviewNote: The finite-net argument needs IID integrability for each center and for the envelope, plus a common almost-sure Lipschitz bound over parameter pairs. Compactness makes the net finite; separability/measurability is stated so the supremum is a legitimate random variable.

lessons.title: Project a method-of-moments estimate onto its parameter space
lessons.reviewNote: Projection consistency requires the population mean to belong to the closed parameter interval and IID integrability for the weak LLN. The final companion deliberately violates feasibility: continuity gives a clipped pseudo-target, not the true mean.
lessons.priorCorrection: Require IID sampling and distinguish the constrained estimator.

lessons.title: Derive the sandwich representation
lessons.reviewNote: The integral Taylor Jacobian must converge along the random segment, which is justified here by consistency, continuity of the expected derivative, and a local uniform derivative LLN (often proved with an integrable envelope). The score CLT separately requires IID sampling, zero mean, and finite covariance; A is defined as minus the derivative limit.

lessons.title: Compute a scalar robust sandwich variance
lessons.reviewNote: The denominator is the square of the derivative sensitivity, while estimator variance is the root-n limit variance divided by n. The displayed standard errors are asymptotic approximations and require the scalar sandwich limit assumptions stated in the formula.

lessons.title: Derive the likelihood information equality
lessons.reviewNote: Information equality uses a correctly specified normalized density on parameter-independent support with two valid differentiations under the integral and finite score moments. Uniform(0,theta) is an explicit counterexample because the support moves, while the misspecified normal example separates expectation under the true law from the working likelihood.

lessons.title: Diagnose boundary and infinite-variance failures
lessons.reviewNote: The boundary normal example has an explicit projection limit with an atom; the symmetric Pareto example has finite first absolute moment but infinite second moment; the cubic score example is identified but has zero Jacobian. Each violates a distinct sandwich hypothesis.

lessons.title: Transfer: sandwich covariance for vector moments
lessons.reviewNote: The vector sandwich has a square nonsingular Jacobian, finite second moment of the moment vector, a consistent root with sufficiently small residual, and a locally uniform derivative LLN. The examples compute covariance rather than standard deviation and preserve the Jacobian sign by using G^{-1} on both sides.

lessons.title: Prove the first-order delta method
lessons.reviewNote: Differentiability is only required at the fixed target. Root-n convergence implies tightness and convergence in probability of Tn to theta0; the Taylor remainder divided by Tn−theta0 is defined as zero on equality and is multiplied by an Op(1) term.

lessons.title: Log transform of a sample mean
lessons.reviewNote: The log is defined only for positive arguments. Nonnegative observations and a positive mean imply positivity of the sample mean with probability tending to one, not necessarily for every finite n; the fallback convention gives a finite-sample statistic and changes no weak limit.
lessons.priorCorrection: Define the log statistic on finite samples with a nonpositive sample mean.

lessons.title: Second-order limit when the first derivative vanishes
lessons.reviewNote: The exact square has a chi-square limit at rate n, while the root-n scaled transform degenerates. The cosine companion checks the general second-order Taylor coefficient g″/2, including a negative limit for a local maximum.

lessons.title: Absolute value at a kink
lessons.reviewNote: The continuous mapping theorem applies at the kink because absolute value is continuous; only the ordinary derivative-based delta theorem fails. The one-sided maximum companion also gives an atom, which the differentiable Gaussian formula would miss.

lessons.title: Variance stabilization for a Bernoulli proportion
lessons.reviewNote: The arcsine derivative cancels the Bernoulli variance only for a fixed interior probability. The transformation is not differentiable with finite derivative at either boundary, so the stabilized normal limit cannot be asserted there without separate asymptotics.

lessons.title: Bootstrap variance of a sample mean
lessons.reviewNote: The empirical bootstrap variance uses the empirical distribution variance with denominator n, not the unbiased n−1 sample variance. The exact conditional identity is algebraic; convergence to population variance separately uses IID sampling and a finite second moment.

lessons.title: Prove the permutation rank and tie argument
lessons.reviewNote: Uniform ranks require the observed assignment to be exchangeable over the full finite orbit under a sharp null. The discrete rank p-value is super-uniform; adding independent uniform jitter is exactly uniform over the orbit, while counting an entire tie block can only make the p-value more conservative.

lessons.title: Compute a two-sided exact treatment permutation p-value
lessons.reviewNote: The enumeration is finite-sample exact only under the sharp null and the stated uniform two-of-four assignment mechanism. The two-sided ordering is explicitly by absolute difference; weak equality of means alone does not imply exchangeability.

lessons.title: Show how dependence defeats iid resampling
lessons.reviewNote: The perfect-dependence counterexample has no finite root-n limit: the scaled actual statistic grows as sqrt(n), whereas the empirical bootstrap is degenerate. The paired and clustered companions separately show that dependence can cause zero, smaller, or larger variance than iid resampling predicts.

lessons.title: Choose resampling by design and null
lessons.reviewNote: The companion counting problem deliberately corrects its stated total: choose(20,6)=38,760; the prompt’s 3,876 is not the assignment-orbit size, and the p-value denominator must use the design orbit. Exact permutation validity is stated for the sharp null, not merely equal means.

lessons.title: Derive the kernel expectation by convolution
lessons.reviewNote: The expansion is an interior-point, small-bandwidth statement; local C2 smoothness alone should be paired with kernel moment and remainder-integrability conditions. A finite h gives an approximation unless the density is locally exactly quadratic or higher terms are separately controlled.

lessons.title: Balance kernel bias and variance
lessons.reviewNote: The optimizer balances squared bias, not bias itself, against variance. Positive leading constants are essential; if the second derivative vanishes or a boundary truncates the kernel window, the n^(-1/5) conclusion may change.

lessons.title: Identify the half-kernel boundary bias
lessons.reviewNote: The boundary limit needs continuity from within the support and an integrable envelope for dominated convergence. The factor one-half is specific to a symmetric kernel; asymmetric kernels retain their own positive-half mass.

lessons.title: Balance three-dimensional kernel error terms
lessons.reviewNote: This rate assumes an interior point and a nonzero second-order bias coefficient. If the leading curvature term vanishes, higher-order bias can alter the rate; at a support boundary the interior expansion is invalid.

lessons.title: Insert Gaussian mode constants into the kernel expansion
lessons.reviewNote: The Gaussian expansion uses local Taylor expansion plus tail domination because the normal density and kernel have unbounded support. The constants are for the standard Gaussian kernel; n^(-1/5) presumes nonzero mode curvature and an interior target.

lessons.title: Prove the two-point Le Cam reduction
lessons.reviewNote: The factor 1/8 comes from both the loss threshold Δ²/4 and averaging the two risks. Total variation is defined here as sup-event probability difference, with no extra factor-of-two convention.

lessons.title: Bound Bernoulli testing difficulty through KL
lessons.reviewNote: The constant 1/192 follows from a uniform TV bound below 1/3, proved using -log(1-x)≤x/(1-x) for x≤1/4 and Pinsker in the convention TV≤sqrt(KL/2). The strictly stronger intermediate inequality is safely weakened at the end.

lessons.title: Interpret a vacuous two-point lower bound
lessons.reviewNote: The two laws with disjoint supports give TV exactly one and a zero right-hand side. The conclusion is lack of a positive lower bound from this inequality, not a general theorem that all estimation problems have zero risk.

lessons.title: Turn a reliable test into an estimator
lessons.reviewNote: The upper bound is exact for the two-valued test-based estimator: its loss is Δ² times the test error indicator. It is a finite parameter-pair statement and should not be generalized to a continuum without further argument.

lessons.title: Derive a minimax rate from close alternatives
lessons.reviewNote: The minimax conclusion applies to any class containing the n-dependent pair and uses the same n-sample laws appearing in the TV premise. The rate is n^-1 only for squared-error loss; the constant c^2/16 is explicit.

lessons.title: Derive Gaussian covariance Frobenius risk
lessons.reviewNote: Known zero mean is essential for the displayed uncentered second-moment estimator; estimating the mean changes finite-sample covariance risk. The sum includes both ordered off-diagonal coordinates in the Frobenius norm.

lessons.title: Derive the deterministic-target shrinkage identity
lessons.reviewNote: The cross-term cancellation requires a deterministic target and an unbiased S (or a separate zero-covariance condition). A random or data-selected target generally leaves a nonzero cross term.

lessons.title: Compute isotropic covariance risk and rank
lessons.reviewNote: The rank statement assumes Gaussian samples with nonsingular covariance and known zero mean, so the data matrix columns are in general position. The p=n case is full rank almost surely, not singular by a degrees-of-freedom denominator convention.

lessons.title: Find when shrinkage toward a poor target hurts
lessons.reviewNote: For V>0 and finite D, the derivative at lambda zero is -2V, so infinitesimal shrinkage cannot increase risk. A fixed small-but-positive weight can hurt when D² exceeds (2/lambda−1)V; this distinction resolves the prompt wording.

lessons.title: Choose the oracle shrinkage weight
lessons.reviewNote: The minimizer is an oracle because it depends on unknown V and target error D² in applications. The boundary cases V=0 or D²=0 are handled by the same formula when the denominator is positive; both zero makes every weight equivalent.

lessons.title: Derive the lasso basic inequality and cone
lessons.reviewNote: The penalty normalization is ||y−Xβ||²/(2n)+λ||β||₁, which fixes the factors 1/2 and 3/2. The cone follows only after dropping Q≥0, and the score condition uses the same n-normalization.

lessons.title: Complete the lasso restricted-eigenvalue bounds
lessons.reviewNote: The restricted eigenvalue is invoked only for Δ in the lasso cone and is stated as sqrt(Q)≥κ||Δ_S||₂. The constants 9 and 12 depend on the exact one-half loss normalization in the basic inequality.

lessons.title: Compute lasso soft thresholding on an orthogonal design
lessons.reviewNote: The stated threshold assumes the loss factor 1/(2n) and design normalization XᵀX/n=I. If the loss omits the one-half or the columns are not normalized, the threshold changes.

lessons.title: Show coefficient nonidentification under collinearity
lessons.reviewNote: The example establishes nonidentification of coefficients, not failure of prediction. Lasso can impose a deterministic tie-breaking convention but that does not recover which duplicate coordinate was truly active.

lessons.title: Translate a score concentration rate into prediction error
lessons.reviewNote: The rate is conditional on the high-probability score event and an RE condition on the cone. The displayed constant is 36c²/κ₀²; big-O suppresses these fixed constants but not the sparsity, dimension logarithm, noise scale, or sample size.

lessons.title: Derive the Beta–Bernoulli posterior
lessons.reviewNote: The binomial coefficient cancels in posterior normalization. Positivity of prior shapes a,b ensures a proper prior; the updated shapes remain positive for all valid counts.

lessons.title: Compute a Beta posterior and predictive probability
lessons.reviewNote: The predictive equality uses the same latent p and conditional iid sampling for the next Bernoulli outcome. Posterior probability about p and predictive probability for a future observation are distinct events, although their numerical values agree here.

lessons.title: Rewrite the posterior mean as weighted shrinkage
lessons.reviewNote: The convergence statement is conditional on the empirical proportion having a limit; under iid Bernoulli(q) sampling it follows almost surely by the strong law. No claim that the finite-n posterior mean equals the sample proportion is made.

lessons.title: Separate posterior mass from frequentist coverage
lessons.reviewNote: Posterior content is conditional and prior-dependent; coverage is a repeated-sampling property at fixed truth. The point-mass examples give exact 0 or 1 coverage, demonstrating that posterior probability statements alone do not guarantee nominal frequentist coverage.

lessons.title: Update odds between two Bernoulli hypotheses
lessons.reviewNote: The formula concerns two simple point hypotheses with positive prior masses and interior Bernoulli probabilities. If a hypothesis assigns a boundary probability 0 or 1, zero likelihood cases need separate treatment rather than ratios with zero denominators.

lessons.title: Prove strong FWER control for Bonferroni and Holm
lessons.reviewNote: Strong control means validity for every configuration of true and false nulls. Holm proof uses the first true-null rank; it does not assume that p-values are independent.

lessons.title: Calculate Bonferroni, Holm, and BH decisions
lessons.reviewNote: All p-values are treated as already sorted increasingly. Holm stops permanently at its first failure; BH uses the largest passing rank, not the first failure. Standard BH guarantee is not assumed under arbitrary dependence.

lessons.title: Interpret the independent Benjamini–Hochberg bound
lessons.reviewNote: The guarantee is BH FDR control under independence (or a separately justified extension) and valid true-null p-values. FDR is E[FDP], with FDP set to zero when R=0; it does not control each realized FDP.

lessons.title: Distinguish FWER from realized false-discovery proportion
lessons.reviewNote: FDP is a realized ratio (with the R=0 convention); FDR is its expectation. FWER is the probability of at least one false rejection. The companion with one false among 100 in every run explicitly shows FDR=.01 but FWER=1.

lessons.title: Match a multiplicity procedure to the goal
lessons.reviewNote: The choice follows the loss function: FWER for any false alarm, FDR for expected false share. Holm/Bonferroni permit arbitrary dependence with valid null p-values; BH here is specifically justified under independence.

lessons.title: Prove the studentized Wald limit
lessons.reviewNote: The variance estimate is for the root-n error, so the standard error of T_n is sqrt(Vhat_n/n). Studentization requires convergence to the same positive V appearing in the numerator CLT.

lessons.title: Calculate a sandwich Wald interval
lessons.reviewNote: All intervals assume Vhat estimates the asymptotic variance of the root-n error. If software instead reports the variance of theta-hat itself, dividing by n again would be incorrect.

lessons.title: Distinguish posterior credibility from confidence coverage
lessons.reviewNote: The no-data example is intentionally exact: a .95 posterior interval under a uniform prior has coverage 1 or 0 depending on the fixed truth. It demonstrates the logical distinction without asserting that all credible sets are miscalibrated.

lessons.title: Compute coverage loss after selecting the largest estimate
lessons.reviewNote: The exact coverage power relies on independent candidate statistics and common cutoff. Using 1.96 gives approximately 0.902508; the exact normal quantile z.975 gives 0.9025, so the two values must not be conflated.
lessons.priorCorrection: Distinguish the rounded 1.96 cutoff from the exact normal quantile.

lessons.title: Audit a post-selection Wald claim
lessons.reviewNote: The claim is deliberately classified as exploratory absent selection-aware calibration. Lasso prediction bounds do not establish nominal post-selection confidence coverage or causal identification.

lessons.title: Derive Bernoulli score, information, and Cramér–Rao bound
lessons.reviewNote: The Cramér–Rao step requires unbiasedness, finite variance, an interior parameter, common support, and differentiation under the integral with score mean zero. The Uniform(0,θ) counterexample has E score≠0 and a moving endpoint, so its smaller unbiased variance does not contradict the regular theorem.

lessons.title: Prove consistency of a constrained quadratic maximizer
lessons.reviewNote: Finite E Z² supplies integrability for the weak law; the population quadratic gap is exact. The interior condition makes the target a point where clipping fixes it, though projection continuity also handles boundary limits.

lessons.title: Derive the two-dimensional kernel rate and boundary warning
lessons.reviewNote: The d=2 rate assumes an interior point, nonzero second-order bias and nh²→∞. The Uniform(0,1) companion explicitly shows the raw symmetric Gaussian KDE converging to half the boundary density.

lessons.title: Derive the lasso cone and prediction bound
lessons.reviewNote: The lasso normalization is one-half squared loss divided by n; changing that convention changes constants. The RE condition is required on the cone, and the duplicate-column companion explicitly demonstrates its failure.

lessons.title: Compute Holm and BH rejections
lessons.reviewNote: Holm halts permanently at its first step-down failure. BH uses the largest passing step-up rank. FWER and FDR are distinct; BH dependence assumptions are stated with the reported result.

lessons.title: Convexity by a segment test
lessons.reviewNote: Checked all three affine inequalities for arbitrary t including endpoints, and verified the simplex barycentric weights and extreme-point argument. Restriction: the proof uses this exact unit-simplex domain and its nonnegative-coordinate constraints.

lessons.title: First-order certificate
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the gradient root, Hessian eigenvalues (2 and 4), strict-convexity uniqueness, and the substituted value -3. Restriction: stationarity gives the global certificate here because the domain is all of R² and the objective is convex.

lessons.title: A flat minimizer set
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the full gradient-zero set, nonnegative objective values, Hessian rank, and the null direction. Restriction: the zero eigenvalue explains nonuniqueness for this quadratic; PSD alone does not guarantee a stationary point exists for every quadratic.

lessons.title: Transfer: a convex function on a convex domain
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the segment stays in C only under domain convexity, and the argument uses differentiability plus the first-order inequality without a Hessian. Restriction: on a nonconvex domain this proof may fail because the connecting path is undefined; no broader conclusion is inferred.

lessons.title: Counterexample: stationary is not enough
lessons.reviewNote: Checked f′(0)=0 and f(1)<f(0), and verified the flat convex example has every point minimizing. Restriction: stationarity is necessary only for an interior differentiable extremum; convexity gives globality, while uniqueness needs an additional condition.

lessons.title: Subdifferential at a kink
lessons.reviewNote: Checked both signs of y in the defining inequality, including y=0 for sufficiency; the interval endpoints are attained supporting slopes. Restriction: this is the scalar absolute-value kink at zero, with the stated extended-real convex subgradient definition.

lessons.title: Solve an ℓ1-penalized scalar problem
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the one-sided derivative signs, subgradient interval [-4,2] at zero, and strict-convexity uniqueness. Restriction: the primary objective is the stated scalar absolute-value penalty plus quadratic; the subgradient sum rule is used with a differentiable smooth summand.

lessons.title: Maximum of affine functions
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the crossing equation x=1, which affine piece is active on each side, and the convex hull of the active slopes. Restriction: the max-of-affine rule is applied to exactly two scalar affine pieces; no differentiability is asserted at the tie.

lessons.title: Transfer: constrained nonsmooth optimum
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the normal-cone sign from its defining inequality at the left endpoint, the objective subgradient {1}, and the cancellation 1+(-1)=0. Restriction: the normal-cone optimality condition is stated for this closed convex interval and this sign convention.

lessons.title: Counterexample: a false smooth derivative rule
lessons.reviewNote: Checked nondifferentiability from unequal one-sided derivatives at zero, the interval subdifferential, and the convex zero-in-subgradient criterion. Restriction: the smooth derivative equation is unavailable at the kink; away from it the subdifferential is a singleton.

lessons.title: Conjugate of a quadratic
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the supremum has a unique maximizer because a>0, substituted the optimizer without dropping the factor 1/2, and matched Fenchel–Young equality to y=ax. Restriction: the formula is finite on all real y only under the stated positive-curvature assumption.

lessons.title: Conjugate of an indicator
lessons.reviewNote: Checked that points outside C contribute negative infinity in the supremum, and that each sign of y selects the correct endpoint; the y=0 tie is handled explicitly. Restriction: C is the stated compact interval, so the support supremum is attained.

lessons.title: Conjugate of absolute value
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the exact dual interval including both endpoints, and the divergence directions for y>1 and y<-1. Restriction: the conjugate is an extended-real indicator; replacing infinity outside the interval by a finite quadratic changes the effective domain.

lessons.title: Transfer: Fenchel dual lower bound
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the opposite signs of the Fenchel–Young inner products and the cancellation, and kept equality unrestricted. Restriction: the bound is weak duality only; no strong-duality claim is made without attainment or qualification.

lessons.title: Counterexample: conjugate domain matters
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the half-line supremum for y=0, y<0, and y>0 separately, and preserved infinity outside the effective domain. Restriction: this is a hard indicator domain; a finite penalty cannot be substituted without changing dual feasibility.

lessons.title: KKT for a one-sided quadratic
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the feasible boundary minimizer, the sign g(x)=-x for x≥0, multiplier λ=1, and complementarity at equality. Restriction: KKT sufficiency uses convex differentiable objective and constraint; no necessity claim beyond this regular scalar case is needed.

lessons.title: Prove the sufficiency argument
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the convex-gradient inequalities, equality cancellation A(y−x*)=0, sign reversal from λ≥0, and the exact use of complementary slackness. Restriction: differentiability and convexity of both f and g are required for the stated supporting inequalities.

lessons.title: Active-set geometry
lessons.reviewNote: Checked coordinatewise projection, the signs of g1=x1−1 and g2=−x2, stationarity coordinates, and both active constraints. Restriction: the projection region is the stated product of half-lines; coordinatewise clamping applies because its constraints separate.

lessons.title: Transfer: constraint qualification failure
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the singleton feasible set, zero constraint gradient, impossible stationarity equation 1=0, and the exact strict-feasibility failure. Restriction: this diagnoses KKT multiplier necessity for the given representation; it does not challenge KKT sufficiency.

lessons.title: Counterexample: complementary slackness is not enough
lessons.reviewNote: Checked primal feasibility, λ≥0, λg=0, the failed stationarity equation, and an explicit feasible point with lower objective. Restriction: complementarity is tested under the g(x)≤0 convention; it is not treated as a stand-alone optimality theorem.

lessons.title: Dual of a constrained quadratic
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the sign convention g(x)=2−x, Lagrangian minimizer x=λ, concave dual maximizer λ=2, and primal value 2. Restriction: this is the specified scalar quadratic with a single lower-bound inequality.

lessons.title: Prove weak duality for equality constraints
lessons.reviewNote: Checked λ_i g_i≤0 for feasible inequalities, the equality residual vanishing for every ν, and the infimum-to-primal-infimum bound direction. Restriction: weak duality requires dual-feasible nonnegative inequality multipliers; ν remains unrestricted.

lessons.title: Sensitivity from a value function
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the active condition u>0, value derivative u, stationarity sign for g=u−x, and the stated multiplier equality. Restriction: the primary comparison is within the positive active regime; companion cases separately check inactive and transition boundaries.

lessons.title: Transfer: certify a lower bound without solving primal
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the bound order q≤p*≤f0(x), dual feasibility of λ=4, and equality of the explicit values 5 for the primal point and dual function. Restriction: a matching certificate requires both candidates feasible; equality is used only after those checks.

lessons.title: Counterexample: Slater can fail to deliver dual attainment
lessons.reviewNote: Checked q(0)=−∞, the λ>0 stationary point and value −1/(4λ), the limit 0, and nonattainment for every finite λ. Restriction: Slater failure is used to explain missing guarantees, not asserted as the sole cause or as a positive duality gap.

lessons.title: Compute the descent certificate
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the update sign, both objective values, and the tight certificate 36/(2·6)=3. Added the necessary segment-containment condition to the formula: an L-Lipschitz gradient on a convex domain does not by itself ensure the gradient step remains in that domain. No convexity of f is invoked.

lessons.title: Derive the descent lemma
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the path integral remainder and its Lipschitz/Cauchy bound Lt||d||², then integrated t over [0,1]. Restriction: the whole segment must lie in the domain where the gradient is L-Lipschitz.

lessons.title: Strong convexity condition number
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the eigenvalue extrema, κ=9, semiaxis ratio √κ=3, and the gradient factors 8/9 and 0. Restriction: these calculations assume the stated symmetric positive-definite quadratic and exact full-gradient updates.

lessons.title: Transfer: prove a linear contraction
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the update matrix, eigenvalue interval [0,1−μ/L], and the required 0<μ≤L restriction for a nonnegative factor. Restriction: the proof applies to the stated exact quadratic Hessian bounds, not to arbitrary nonsmooth objectives.

lessons.title: Counterexample: oversized steps oscillate and grow
lessons.reviewNote: Checked xₙ₊₁=−1.2xₙ, the two objective values, and the stability boundary |1−η|=1. Restriction: this counterexample uses the one-dimensional unit-curvature quadratic; it shows smoothness alone cannot justify an oversized step.

lessons.title: Soft-threshold coordinates
lessons.reviewNote: Checked threshold γλ=1, the signs of all coordinates, and the equality/strict-threshold zero cases. Restriction: the coordinate formula assumes the separable ℓ1 penalty, λ≥0, and γ>0.

lessons.title: Derive the proximal optimality condition
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the gradient sign, division by γ>0, and the nonsmooth inclusion form; the quadratic guarantees uniqueness. Restriction: h must be proper, lower-semicontinuous and convex for the stated exact subgradient characterization.

lessons.title: Prove firm nonexpansiveness
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the subgradient inequality directions, monotonicity expression, multiplication by γ>0, and final rearrangement. Restriction: convexity is essential for monotonicity; the proof does not cover nonconvex proximal objectives.

lessons.title: Transfer: prox for a half-line indicator
lessons.reviewNote: Checked projection cases v≥0 and v<0, especially v=0 at the boundary, and the normal-cone sign N(0)=(-∞,0]. Restriction: the formula uses the closed convex half-line indicator and γ>0.

lessons.title: Counterexample: a nonconvex prox can be set-valued
lessons.reviewNote: Checked both completed-square branches, their equal minimum −1/2, and the distinct nonconvex examples. Restriction: without convexity, a proximal argmin may be multiple or fail to exist; no single-valued-map theorem is claimed.

lessons.title: Choose the regret-optimal constant step
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the derivative, strict convexity of the scalar bound, η*=3/20, total bound 60, and average 0.6. Restriction: the formula assumes positive D,G,T and the stated constant-step bound.

lessons.title: Derive the one-step potential inequality
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the projection VI sign, expansion cross-term sign, telescoping distance terms, and the comparator membership restriction. Restriction: the comparator must belong to the closed convex set C.

lessons.title: Compute a projected stochastic step
lessons.reviewNote: Checked tentative update 0.6 remains feasible, the potential values 1.69 and 0.01, and the unprojected identity. Restriction: the primary calculation is one realized step; it is not an expected-regret guarantee.

lessons.title: Transfer: identify the bias term
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the sign in grad=E[g|F]−b, the Cauchy–Schwarz bound βD, and the cumulative/average factors T. Restriction: the claim requires bounded bias, bounded comparator distance, and the stated conditional second-moment bound.

lessons.title: Counterexample: unbounded gradients destroy the stated bound
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the Bernoulli mean M·(1/M)=1 and second moment M²·(1/M)=M. Restriction: the failure is uniformity of the second-moment bound as M grows; each fixed M remains finite.

lessons.title: Condition number from singular values
lessons.reviewNote: Checked σmax/σmin=500, the squared value 250,000, and the amplification ratio 500. Restriction: A must have full column rank; otherwise σmin=0 and AᵀA is singular.

lessons.title: Prove the singular-value identity
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the thin-SVD multiplication, squared singular spectrum, and the role of σmin>0; rank deficiency makes the normal matrix singular. Restriction: the finite identity requires full column rank; infinity is only the extended-condition interpretation.

lessons.title: Backward versus forward error
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the fixed-A compatible bound with relative residual ηb, the missing ||b|| scale, and the first-order Eᵀr term for inconsistent least squares. Added full column rank to the perturbation companion because its displayed formula uses (AᵀA)⁻¹ and the least-squares solution must be unique. Restriction: the κ-scaled bound is for compatible systems with fixed A; perturbing A in inconsistent least squares changes the sensitivity model.

lessons.title: Transfer: QR least squares
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the orthogonal decomposition, constant residual term, and triangular solve condition R nonsingular. Restriction: the result uses reduced QR with orthonormal Q columns; normal-equation conditioning is not assumed benign.

lessons.title: Counterexample: residual hides an ill-conditioned direction
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the exact solution, unit parameter error, residual ε, and limit ε→0+ while κ=1/ε grows. Restriction: ε remains positive; at ε=0 the system loses full column rank and a unique exact solution is not guaranteed.

lessons.title: Gradient certificate calculation
lessons.reviewNote: Checked 0.04²=0.0016 and 2μ=1. Restriction: requires differentiability, μ>0, global strong convexity on the convex feasible domain, and an attained minimum; the reported quantity is an upper bound, not the exact gap.

lessons.title: Prove the gap bound by completing a square
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the rearrangement sign, the μ-scaled square center d=a/μ, and that the discarded term is nonpositive only for μ>0. Restriction: strong convexity must hold on a convex domain containing x and x*; constrained boundary minimizers are allowed, but the minimum must exist.

lessons.title: Build a scaled KKT residual report
lessons.reviewNote: Recomputed both constraint values, multiplier signs, stationarity vector and Euclidean norm, and both signed products before taking absolute values. Restriction: these are unscaled diagnostics under the stated sign convention; objective/constraint rescaling changes magnitudes, and no combined score is defined.

lessons.title: Transfer: a noisy gradient certificate
lessons.reviewNote: Checked triangle-inequality direction, nonnegative squaring, and substitution of the true-gradient bound into the strong-convexity theorem. Restriction: ε must be a valid norm-error bound at this iterate, μ>0 must hold globally, and the result is conservative rather than an estimate of the exact gap.

lessons.title: Counterexample: a small gradient in a flat region
lessons.reviewNote: Checked f′=4x³, f″=12x², endpoint evaluations, and the zero curvature infimum at x=0. Restriction: the failure is for a fixed global μ>0 on R; on domains bounded away from zero (for example [1,∞)) the same function has a positive strong-convexity constant.

lessons.title: One proximal-gradient iterate
lessons.reviewNote: Recomputed the gradient proposal, threshold ηλ, and full composite values at both iterates. Restriction: the example uses the stated unit smoothness; soft thresholding returns zero whenever |v|≤ηλ.

lessons.title: Derive proximal-gradient optimality
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the square-completion constant, prox center, and Fermat inclusion signs. Restriction: η>0 and h proper closed convex; at an ℓ1 zero coordinate the subgradient is an interval.

lessons.title: Prove the telescoping objective bound
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the telescoping endpoints x₁ and x_{T+1}, the sign of the dropped terminal square, division by T, and the indexing of the averaged points. Restriction: Jensen requires F convex and the one-step inequality must hold for every step.

lessons.title: Transfer: choose the split that makes prox cheap
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the gradient, Hessian norm, threshold scale, and the degenerate A=0 case where 1/L is undefined. Restriction: λ≥0 is assumed for convex LASSO; the standard smooth-step bound uses L>0 or any positive upper Lipschitz bound.

lessons.title: Counterexample: unsafe proximal step
lessons.reviewNote: Checked x⁺=(1−η)x, objective ratio (1−η)², and the distinction between a sufficient η≤1/L guarantee and the quadratic decrease interval 0<η<2/L. Restriction: the ratio formula assumes x≠0; the zero iterate is unchanged.

lessons.title: Box quadratic certificate and ill-scaled SPD transfer
lessons.reviewNote: Checked Lagrangian signs for upper/lower box constraints, stationarity, complementarity, and q=P=0.5. Recomputed both diagonal solves and relative perturbations. Restriction: exact zero residual is for the perturbed right side in exact arithmetic; it does not undo data sensitivity.

lessons.title: Equality-constrained ridge duality and gradient descent
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the Lagrange multiplier sign, dual constant −νd, KKT equality solution and matching values. For ridge, verified λ≤h_j≤L and squared eigenmode factors. Restriction: λ>0 ensures strict convexity; the stated contraction is for the fixed step 1/L.

lessons.title: Numerical choice under ill-conditioning
lessons.reviewNote: Recomputed both singular-value ratios, the perturbed coordinate solution, relative perturbation norms, and scaled-residual denominator. Restriction: QR/SVD improves algorithmic stability but cannot remove forward sensitivity inherent in a large condition number.

lessons.title: Form A — prove a Fenchel certificate for LASSO
lessons.reviewNote: Checked both conjugates, the minus sign in h*(−Aᵀu), and equality condition −Aᵀu∈∂h(x). For λ>0, g is continuous everywhere and h is finite everywhere, so the Fenchel–Rockafellar qualification holds. Restriction: the stated equal-value pair is a sufficient certificate, not a claim that every candidate x already supplies one.

lessons.title: Schur complement and constrained sensitivity
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the KKT stationarity sign against the chosen +λᵀ(Ax−b) convention, primal feasibility, positive definiteness of S under full row rank, and ∇v=−λ*. Restriction: dependent equality rows make S singular even when the feasible primal minimizer exists.

lessons.title: Autocovariance and PSD check
lessons.reviewNote: Checked γ(±1), both signed geometric tails, convergence for |φ|<1, and positivity of (1+φ)/(1−φ), including negative φ. Restriction: Ω is the covariance sum under this AR(1)-form sequence; a generic sequence needs its own summability/validity assumptions.

lessons.title: Prove the sample-mean variance formula
lessons.reviewNote: Checked ordered-pair counts n−|h| for positive and negative lags, the n² denominator, and the n multiplier yielding Bartlett weights. Restriction: the identity uses weak stationarity and finite second moments; no independence assumption is needed.

lessons.title: Weak but not strict stationarity
lessons.reviewNote: Checked within-block pairwise independence, cross-block independence, constant mean/variance and zero nonzero-lag covariance; the alternating block triple product changes law under a three-step shift. Restriction: weak stationarity does not imply strict stationarity without distributional assumptions.

lessons.title: Prove covariance matrices are PSD
lessons.reviewNote: Expanded aᵀΓa as the variance of aᵀX and checked the finite-moment premise. Companion quadratic forms include both a PSD example and an explicit negative-variance contradiction. Restriction: negative eigenvalues from rounded estimates should be interpreted by scale and construction method.

lessons.title: Transfer: long-run variance under absolute summability
lessons.reviewNote: Verified pointwise convergence of Bartlett weights, domination by |γ(h)|, and the exact assumption Σ|γ(h)|<∞. Restriction: this yields convergence of scaled variances, not a CLT or a distributional approximation.

lessons.title: Yule–Walker values
lessons.reviewNote: Recomputed 1−φ²=0.36, γ₀=4, and powers φ and φ³; checked the |φ|<1 premise before using the stationary variance formula. Restriction: σ² is innovation variance, not marginal variance.

lessons.title: Derive Yule–Walker for AR(1)
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the positive-lag covariance index h−1 and kept h=0 separate, where E[εₜXₜ]=σ² under orthogonality to the past. Restriction: the recurrence requires zero-mean stationarity and innovation orthogonality; it is not implied by the AR equation alone.

lessons.title: Causality and invertibility roots
lessons.reviewNote: Checked each polynomial under the declared lag convention and compared root moduli strictly with one. Restriction: an inside AR root rules out a causal representation but can permit an anti-causal stationary solution; an MA root test addresses invertibility, not finite-MA stationarity.

lessons.title: Transfer: nonstationary differenced series
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the difference operator, IID increment moments, level variance and min(s,t) covariance. Restriction: conclusions use fixed or independent initial level and σ²>0; stationary theorems for levels do not transfer to increments without reformulating the target.

lessons.title: Counterexample: structural break versus unit root
lessons.reviewNote: Checked fixed-date deterministic means versus accumulated innovation variance, and qualified the result for an uncertain break date. Restriction: the constant-variance claim is conditional on a fixed mean path; random break timing can add mixture variance.

lessons.title: Spectrum of a two-tap filter
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the complex-conjugate product, values at 0 and π, and the 1/(2π) normalization against γ(0)=5. Restriction: frequencies are in radians on [−π,π]; this density convention integrates to variance.

lessons.title: Derive filter covariance and spectrum
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the matching-index condition k=j−h, the conjugate response product, and absolute-summability use for rearranging sums. Restriction: the stated real-coefficient formula uses white, uncorrelated innovations and the 1/(2π) spectral convention.

lessons.title: Recover variance by integrating spectrum
lessons.reviewNote: Checked termwise integration under absolute covariance summability, the full-period orthogonality factor 2π, and the 1/(2π) normalization. Restriction: one-sided integration equals half the variance only for an even density and requires doubling.

lessons.title: Transfer: long-run variance is zero-frequency power
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the absolute-summability condition, the 2π relation at zero frequency, and agreement of AR geometric sums with the spectral formula for positive and negative φ. Restriction: Ω is finite under |φ|<1; at a unit root the covariance series does not converge.

lessons.title: Counterexample: a unit root has no ordinary stationary density
lessons.reviewNote: Checked the random-walk sum, variance growth, min(s,t) covariance, and the white-noise density convention for increments. Restriction: the ordinary Fourier spectral density is for stationary levels; the flat density here applies only to the differenced process.
lessons.priorCorrection: Summable covariances are sufficient for the Fourier formula, not necessary for every spectral density.

lessons.title: Mixing and moment check
lessons.reviewNote: Checked exponent, geometric ratio, k≥1 range and δ-to-moment match. Restriction: CLT is assumed, needs strict stationarity and centering, and is nondegenerate only for Ω>0.

lessons.title: Prove LLN from a variance rate
lessons.reviewNote: Corrected the Chebyshev step: n Var(X̄ₙ) tends to Ω, not zero; with fixed ε>0 the denominator nε² diverges, so the ratio vanishes. Checked centering and the rate limit. Restriction: variance controls spread from E[X̄ₙ], so E[X̄ₙ]=μ is essential; a positive limit is not a CLT.

lessons.title: Zero long-run variance through telescoping
lessons.reviewNote: Checked lag-zero variance, opposite-sign lag-one terms, cutoff and telescoping variance. Restriction: finite second moments suffice; Ω=0 means a degenerate normalized limit.

lessons.title: Transfer: verify hypotheses on a finite-dependent Gaussian model
lessons.reviewNote: Checked exact innovation-index separation at k≥2, Gaussian moment availability, finite mixing sum and covariance factorization. Restriction: σ²>0 and θ≠−1 ensure Ω>0; the CLT is assumed.

lessons.title: Counterexample: pairwise zero covariance is not independence
lessons.reviewNote: Checked all means and pairwise product expectations, then used the sure relation for dependence. Restriction: zero pairwise covariance is not joint independence and does not imply event mixing.

lessons.title: Bartlett HAC arithmetic
lessons.reviewNote: Recomputed Bartlett weights, lag-pair factor two, exact fraction 17/6 and final rounding. Restriction: this is the finite-bandwidth estimate; it is not identified with Ω without asymptotic assumptions.

lessons.title: Prove Bartlett positive semidefiniteness
lessons.reviewNote: Checked zero-padding, lag-pair count b+1−|h|, autocovariance symmetry and especially divisor n(b+1). Restriction: the PSD identity applies to the stated common-window Bartlett estimator, not arbitrary truncation.
lessons.priorCorrection: Carry 1/n through the entire Bartlett derivation.

lessons.title: Derive the sandwich from an asymptotic linearization
lessons.reviewNote: Checked covariance transformation order, nonsingularity of A, Slutsky remainder, and consistency needed for estimated A. Restriction: IID information is valid only when its covariance identity matches Ω.

lessons.title: Transfer: overlapping forecast losses
lessons.reviewNote: Counted target-window intersections and retained the A−B matched-origin estimand. Restriction: overlap permits serial dependence but is not sufficient to prove nonzero covariance; HAC/block validity needs process assumptions.

lessons.title: Counterexample: truncated covariance can be negative
lessons.reviewNote: Recomputed raw −0.6 and Bartlett 0.2 with the b=1 weight 1/2. Restriction: nonnegativity follows from Bartlett’s quadratic-form construction and does not generalize to arbitrary truncation.

lessons.title: Construct one block resample
